title: Rules-Based vs. Machine Learning Credit Models: A Lender's Guide
summary: Rules are easier to explain, and ML can find more risk signal. Many lenders combine both: rules set policy, and models rank risk.
body_markdown:
Every lender has to decide how credit decisions get made. The rules based vs machine learning credit models question often comes up when teams launch a product or see approval rates stall.


This guide explains how each approach works, where each one falls short, and which U.S. rules apply as of November 2026. It ends with a practical way to choose and test. It is educational content—not legal advice.


‍


### What's the difference between rules-based and machine learning credit models?


A rules-based credit model makes decisions using criteria and weights that people write and set by hand. A machine learning credit model learns patterns from past loan outcomes and uses them to predict who will repay. Many lenders run both in the same decision flow.


That makes the choice an operational one. The real question is which decisions belong to fixed rules and which belong to a model that learns from data.


- **Rules are written by people:** A credit analyst sets each cutoff, so every decision traces back to a known rule.
- **ML models are trained on data:** An algorithm finds the patterns, so the logic lives inside the model.
- **Both can work together:** Rules often screen applicants first, and a model then ranks the risk of those who pass.


‍


### How rules-based credit models work


A rules-based credit model uses logic that a person can read line by line. It comes in two main forms: policy rules and scorecards.


Policy rules are IF-THEN statements. For example, "IF the business has been open less than 12 months, THEN decline." Rules that end an application on the spot are called knockout rules.


A credit scorecard is different. It gives points for each borrower trait, such as time in business or payment history, and adds them into one score. Scorecards are commonly built with logistic regression—a statistical method that estimates the odds of a yes-or-no outcome, like default.


Some lenders also use decision trees. A decision tree splits applicants into groups through a series of simple questions. If you want the step-by-step process, see our guide on[how to build a credit scorecard](https://www.lendflow.com/post/how-to-build-a-credit-scorecard) .


Rules-based models are deterministic. That means the same inputs always produce the same output, which makes them easy to audit.


- **Policy rules decide eligibility:** They answer "Can we lend to this applicant at all?"
- **Scorecards rank risk:** They answer "How likely is this applicant to repay?"


#### Where rules-based models fall short


Rules and scorecards work best with a short list of well-known inputs. That strength turns into a limit when borrowers or markets change.


- **Limited inputs:** Scorecards often use a limited set of variables, so useful signals in other data can go unused.
- **Slow to adapt:** Each change needs a person to rewrite a rule or rebuild the scorecard.
- **Missed patterns:** Simple rules struggle with nonlinear patterns, where two traits matter only in combination.
- **Thin-file gaps:** Applicants with little credit history give rules very little to work with.


A thin-file borrower has few accounts on a credit report. A credit-invisible borrower has no credit record at a nationwide bureau at all. According to the[CFPB credit invisibles update](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/data-research/research-reports/technical-correction-and-update-to-the-cfpbs-credit-invisibles-estimate/) , about 2.7 percent of U.S. adults were credit invisible in 2020.


The CFPB cut its earlier estimate roughly in half, but thin files are still common. Some lenders look to alternative data—such as bank account cash flow—to fill the gap.


‍


### How machine learning credit models work


A machine learning (ML) credit model learns from examples. You feed it past applications and what happened next, and it finds the patterns that link the two.


Machine learning credit scoring is usually framed as supervised binary classification. "Supervised" means each past loan has a known label. "Binary" means there are two labels: good (repaid) or bad (defaulted).


The model then predicts the chance that a new applicant lands in the "bad" group. That number is often called a probability of default. Our guide to[probability of default models](https://www.lendflow.com/post/how-to-build-and-deploy-probability-of-default-models) covers how lenders build and deploy them.


Common ML methods include:


- **Gradient boosting (such as XGBoost):** Builds many small decision trees, with each new tree fixing errors from the last.
- **Random forests:** Builds many trees on random slices of the data, then averages their votes.
- **Neural networks:** Passes data through layers of connected nodes to find complex patterns.


Gradient boosting and random forests are ensembles, which means they combine many simple models into one. The[Dastile credit scoring survey](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1568494620302039) reviewed 74 studies from 2010 to 2018 and found that ensembles generally beat single classifiers.


The same survey found no agreement on one best model. It also flagged that some ML models cannot explain their predictions.


#### What ML models need to perform


ML models are only as good as the data behind them. Before you train one, check four needs.


- **Large, clean, labeled data:** The model needs many past loans with accurate outcomes and consistent fields.
- **A plan for imbalanced data:** Defaults are usually rare, so the model may learn to predict "good" for everyone.
- **Reject inference:** You only see outcomes for approved loans, so you must estimate how declined applicants would have performed.
- **Ongoing monitoring:** Borrower behavior shifts over time, an effect called drift, so models need regular checks.


Data quality starts upstream. Pulling bureau, bank, and business data into one clean record is the work of[financial data aggregation for underwriting](https://www.lendflow.com/post/financial-data-aggregation-for-underwriting-a-practical-guide) .


‍


### Rules based vs machine learning credit models: side-by-side comparison


Each approach trades something for something else. ML can find more signal in some datasets, while rules are typically easier to explain, change, and govern.


How big is the accuracy gap? One 2025[FinRegLab ML underwriting study](https://finreglab.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/FinRegLab_07-01-2025_Advancing-the-Credit-Ecosystem-Factsheet.pdf) compared XGBoost with logistic regression built on the same data. ML improved predictive accuracy by up to 2% and raised approval rates by as much as 4% in simulations.


Those figures come from one dataset, so treat them as a sign of what's possible. Your results will depend on your product, borrowers, and data.


Factor Rules-based (policy rules and scorecards) Machine learning (e.g., XGBoost, random forest)


Accuracy Typically solid on well-known inputs Can be higher, depending on the data


Explainability Typically high—each factor and weight is visible Typically lower—may need added explanation tools


Data needs Typically works with smaller, simpler datasets Typically needs a large, clean, labeled history


Speed to change Typically fast for one rule; slower to rebuild a scorecard Retraining typically takes data work and testing


Governance effort Typically lighter for pure policy rules Typically heavier validation and monitoring


Adverse action readiness Reasons typically map to rules or score factors Reasons typically must be drawn from the model and checked


Bias risk Cutoffs are easier to review but can still carry bias A variable like ZIP code can act as a proxy for a protected trait


The table is a general, qualitative guide. The accuracy row reflects the FinRegLab study and the Dastile survey above, and the governance row reflects SR 26-2, covered below.


**Key point:** Neither column wins every row. The best fit depends on which rows matter most for your product.


‍


### Regulatory considerations for both model types


U.S. lending rules don't care which technology made the decision. They care whether the decision was fair and whether the borrower got a clear reason.


Three areas matter most: adverse action notices, fair lending, and model risk management. The status below is current as of November 2026, so confirm details with counsel before you act.


#### Adverse action notices under ECOA and Regulation B


The Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA) bans discrimination in lending. Regulation B is the rule that puts ECOA into practice. An adverse action is a negative decision, such as a decline or a worse offer than requested.


Under the[Regulation B notification rules](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/12/1002.9) , consumer credit applicants generally must be notified within 30 days of a completed application. The stated reasons must be specific and indicate the principal reasons for the decision.


Business credit applicants have different notice rules under §1002.9(a)(3).


Reg B also says a vague reason—such as failing internal standards or missing a qualifying score—is not enough. That applies to rules, scorecards, and ML alike. Other deadlines apply in some cases, such as counteroffers and existing accounts.


In 2022, the CFPB took a clear view on complex algorithms. The[CFPB 2022 adverse action circular](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/compliance/circulars/circular-2022-03-adverse-action-notification-requirements-in-connection-with-credit-decisions-based-on-complex-algorithms/) said these requirements apply equally to all credit decisions, regardless of the technology used.


The CFPB later pulled that guidance. Its[CFPB withdrawn guidance list](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/compliance/guidance/withdrawn-guidance/) shows Circulars 2022-03 and 2023-03 were withdrawn on May 12, 2025.


**Key point:** The withdrawals removed the CFPB's commentary only. The duty to give specific reasons comes from the Regulation B text itself (12 CFR §1002.9), which still governs.


#### Fair lending and model risk management


Fair lending risk includes disparate impact. That happens when a neutral-looking policy harms a protected group more than others without a strong business reason.


ML models raise a specific concern here. For example, a variable like ZIP code can act as a proxy for a protected trait such as race—even without race as an input. Rules can carry this risk too, but their cutoffs are easier to review.


Model risk management is the process of making sure models work as intended. The[SR 26-2 model risk guidance](https://www.federalreserve.gov/supervisionreg/srletters/SR2602.pdf) , issued April 17, 2026, supersedes and replaces SR 11-7.


SR 26-2 is non-binding, risk-based guidance from the Federal Reserve, OCC, and FDIC. It is most relevant to banking organizations with over $30 billion in assets.


Its "model" definition excludes deterministic rule-based processes with no statistical theory behind them. So a simple knockout rule may fall outside it, while statistical scorecards and ML models likely fall inside. SR 26-2 also excludes generative and agentic AI from its scope.


**Key point:** Governance effort differs by model type. In practice, fintechs that lend through partner banks may feel these expectations through those partners.


‍


### The hybrid approach: rules for policy, models for risk ranking


Many lenders blend both approaches in one decision flow. Rules handle the fixed policy questions, and a model handles the risk question.


This framing is a practical design pattern drawn from how lenders operate. It's a starting point you'll shape to your own credit policy.


A typical hybrid flow inside a[credit decision engine](https://www.lendflow.com/post/decision-engine) looks like this:


1. **Eligibility and compliance rules:** Knockout rules screen out applicants who fail hard policy limits.
2. **Risk ranking:** A scorecard or ML model scores the applicants who pass.
3. **Pricing and limits:** Rules turn the score into an offer, rate, and credit line.
4. **Reason codes:** The flow records the main factors behind each decision for adverse action notices.
5. **Decline routing:** Declined applicants move to other capital providers that may fit.


Reason codes are short statements of the top factors behind a decision. Your model owners still need a reliable, validated way to produce them for each model.


Decline routing gives a declined applicant another path to funding. A[credit decline waterfall](https://www.lendflow.com/post/credit-waterfall) sends a declined applicant to the next lender or product in line.


Lendflow focuses on the data side of this flow.[Lendflow's underwriting and decisioning tools](https://www.lendflow.com/solutions/credit-underwriting-and-decisioning) include Data Orchestration, which connects lenders with integration partners and supports decline waterfalls.


The product suite also includes Data Decisioning Tools and Lendflow Intelligence. The platform supports live credit signals, so rules and models can act on current data.


‍


### How to choose and test your credit model approach


There's no single right answer to rules based vs machine learning credit models for every lender. Start by scoring your situation against a few questions.


- **Data volume:** Do you have thousands of past loans with clear outcomes? If not, start with rules and a scorecard.
- **Explainability needs:** Must every decision be easy to explain to borrowers, partners, and examiners? Weight rules and simpler models higher.
- **Regulatory exposure:** Do you lend through a partner bank or as a large bank? Plan for model validation and documentation.
- **Team capacity:** Do you have data scientists to build, validate, and monitor ML models? If not, ML adds risk.


Once you have a candidate, test it before a full switch. Champion-challenger testing compares your current approach (the champion) with a new one (the challenger) on a small share of applicants.


The[OCC credit card lending handbook](https://www.occ.treas.gov/publications-and-resources/publications/comptrollers-handbook/files/credit-card-lending/pub-ch-credit-card.pdf) notes that banks often use a champion-challenger technique to test account management initiatives. It describes running tests on smaller parts of a portfolio, usually for several months.


After launch, keep watching. Track approval rates, default rates, and score shifts each month so you catch drift early.


Monitoring is easier when your workflow runs on its own. Learn how[automated credit decisioning](https://www.lendflow.com/post/automated-credit-decisioning) helps teams scale decisions without adding manual review.

### FAQ


#### Is machine learning more accurate than a credit scorecard?


It can be, but the gain varies by dataset—one 2025 FinRegLab study found ML improved predictive accuracy by up to 2% over logistic regression. Results depend on your data quality, product, and borrowers.


#### Can lenders use ML models and still meet adverse action rules?


Yes, as long as the lender can give each declined applicant specific, accurate principal reasons, as Regulation B requires. The technology used doesn't change that duty.


#### What is a black-box credit model?


A black-box model is one whose inner logic can be hard for people to see or explain, such as a large neural network. Lenders using one may need added tools and validation to explain its decisions.


#### Why do lenders still use logistic regression?


Logistic regression is often simpler and easier to explain, which can make adverse action reasons and audits more straightforward. It can also work well with smaller datasets.


#### What is champion-challenger testing?


Champion-challenger testing runs a new strategy (the challenger) against the current one (the champion) on a small share of accounts. Lenders compare results over time before rolling out the winner.
